recipe.history:
Guacamole is one of the Western Hemisphere's great culinary inheritances, originating with the Aztec peoples of central Mexico where avocados — ahuacatl in Nahuatl — had been cultivated in Mesoamerica for at least five thousand years before Spanish contact. The earliest forms of guacamole were simple: avocado crushed in a molcajete with salt, tomato, and chili, eaten as a dip or condiment at the heart of Aztec cuisine. Chicory — Cichorium intybus — has an entirely different lineage, native to Europe and the Mediterranean basin, where its bitter leaves have been eaten since ancient Egypt and its roasted root has been used as a coffee substitute since the Napoleonic era, when a continental blockade cut off French coffee supplies. Hickory, the North American hardwood, contributes a third thread: its dense, slow-burning wood produces a smoke with a sweet, bacon-like backbone that has been central to Southern and Appalachian barbecue since Indigenous peoples first used it to smoke and preserve meat. These three flavors — the fat green creaminess of avocado, the clean radicchio-like bitterness of chicory, and the sweet deep smoke of hickory — form a triangle of contrast that makes each element more vivid by comparison.

Guacamole arrived on American burgers via the California taco-bar crossover culture of the late 1970s, when avocado toast's predecessor — the avocado burger — appeared on menus in Los Angeles as a health-food inflected take on fast food. Chicory's bitterness arrived in burger culture from the salad world: as mesclun and bitter greens became fashionable in the 1990s, chefs began using radicchio and endive to add complexity to burgers where iceberg had once been a given. Hickory smoke arrived as a flavoring — in liquid smoke, in smoked salts, in hickory-smoked cheddar — when backyard grilling culture and craft barbecue began cross-pollinating with restaurant cooking in the 2000s. A hickory-smoked salt rubbed into a beef patty before cooking replicates the slow perfume of a barbecue pit in a cast-iron skillet, giving the guac-and-chicory combination a savory, woodsy foundation it would otherwise lack.

I learned to make guacamole from a woman who sold it at a small stand in a farmers' market, and she told me that the single greatest error people make is adding too much. Too much lime drowns the avocado. Too much onion turns it sharp. Too much cilantro makes it taste like soap to half the people who eat it. The art is restraint: you want to taste avocado first, then the heat of jalapeño, then the acid of lime as a brightening afterthought. I have made guacamole hundreds of times since then and I still hear her voice when I reach for the lime. The chicory on this burger was my own addition — something I discovered by accident when I ran out of arugula and grabbed the wrong bag from the refrigerator, and found that the bitterness did something to the guacamole's fat that lime alone never could: it cleaned the palate between bites so that each mouthful felt as vivid as the first.

The case for medium rare is the case for the avocado on top of it. Guacamole placed on a well-done patty slowly warms into something flat and dull: the delicate vegetal quality of the avocado cooks away, the lime acid sharpens without fat to soften it, and the whole topping becomes heavy and one-dimensional. A medium rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is warm enough to take the chill off the guacamole without cooking it, allowing the cold creaminess of the avocado to meet the warm richness of the beef in a temperature contrast that makes both more interesting. This is not coincidence; it is physics. The burger is a controlled environment, and the cook who controls it deserves the best possible outcome.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
1 small plum tomato, seeded and finely diced
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 large head chicory (or radicchio), cored and thinly shredded
1 small head Belgian endive, thinly sliced
900g freshly ground beef (80% chuck, 20% brisket blend)
instructions: 1. Make the chicory slaw (at least 30 minutes ahead): Whisk together olive oil, apple cider vinegar, honey, and Dijon mustard in a large bowl until emulsified. Season with salt and pepper. Add shredded chicory and sliced endive, toss to coat evenly, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes to allow the bitterness to mellow slightly in the acid.

2. Make the brioche buns: Combine bread flour, instant yeast, salt, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl with a dough hook. Add 2 eggs and warm milk and mix on low for 2 minutes. Knead on medium for 5 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time, fully incorporating each addition. Knead on medium-high for 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

3. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 6 portions of about 100g, shape into tight balls, place on parchment-lined baking sheets, and proof covered for 45 minutes.
4. Preheat oven to 190°C (375°F). Brush buns with egg wash (remaining egg plus 1 tablespoon water) and bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.
5. Make the hickory-smoked rub: Combine smoked sea salt, smoked paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, and cracked black pepper in a small bowl. Mix well.

6. Make the guacamole: Halve and pit the avocados. Scoop the flesh into a bowl and mash with a fork to a chunky consistency — do not purée. Add lime juice, minced jalapeño, diced onion, cilantro, and diced tomato. Season with kosher salt. Taste and adjust acid and heat. Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface of the guacamole and refrigerate until needed.

7. Form the beef patties: Divide ground beef into 6 equal portions of 150g each. Handle minimally. Form each into a 10cm-wide, 2cm-thick patty with a thumb indent in the center. Press the hickory rub generously into both faces of each patty immediately before cooking.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties undisturbed for 3 minutes. Flip once. Place a slice of smoked Gouda on each patty immediately. Cook for 2–2.5 more minutes. Check the center with an instant-read thermometer — target is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes.
9. Slice brioche buns and toast cut-side down in a buttered skillet over medium heat for 60–90 seconds.

10. Assemble each burger: Place two tomato slices on the bottom bun. Set the rested smoked Gouda-topped patty on top. Spoon a generous mound of guacamole directly onto the patty. Top the guacamole with a well-drained handful of chicory slaw. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and press the top bun gently on. Serve immediately.
